strengths: The paper proposes an intuitive and lightweight way to inspect linear-probe weights on top of foundation-model embeddings, connecting weight drift from class-name embeddings to possible spurious concepts.

weaknesses: The evaluation is not convincing enough for the main claims. The paper mainly validates bias discovery indirectly via zero-shot prompt augmentation, without measuring precision/recall of identified biases, human validation, or downstream debiasing of the trained model.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete: several competing methods are missing on Nico++ and CivilComments, and there are no strong random/common-concept/prompt-ensemble controls to show that the gains come specifically from ConceptDrift.

The multiclass scoring rule uses the minimum similarity over other classes rather than the maximum competing class, so it does not directly correspond to a classification margin and can rank concepts that distinguish a class from only one weak competitor.

The method still relies heavily on captioning, keyword extraction, WordNet filtering, and prompt templates, so the claim of moving beyond data-restricted protocols is overstated. Reproducibility is also limited by missing implementation details, seeds, uncertainty estimates, and cutoff-selection protocol.

Baselines and comparisons are incomplete. Several tables omit relevant methods on some datasets, compare against methods in settings where they are structurally disadvantaged, and do not provide enough detail to know whether baselines were fairly tuned or adapted.

The mitigation and zero-shot prompting experiments are not strong validation of detection quality. Adding discovered concepts to prompts can improve worst-group accuracy on known-biased datasets, but average accuracy sometimes drops substantially, and the result does not prove that the extracted concepts are complete, precise, or learned by the target model.

Reproducibility is poor: the abstract has an unfinished code-availability statement, LLM filtering prompts and decisions are missing, FLUX generation details and seeds are absent, key hyperparameters such as the thresholding window are underspecified, and the ImageNet concept lists are promised only upon acceptance.
The writing overclaims throughout, repeatedly stating that the method surpasses state of the art and exposes previously untapped ImageNet correlations despite limited and cherry-picked evidence.

Ethical and misuse considerations are underdeveloped, especially given that the paper explicitly demonstrates how identified concepts can be used to generate images that fool deployed classifiers and touches on sensitive demographic/fairness-related datasets.
